questions.article: Condemnation of Attack on Charlie Hebdo in Paris
questions.q: In condemning the attack in Paris, what does the editorial say the Prophet and his Companions did when they themselves were ridiculed?
options: They answered every insult with an insult
Not quite. The article says: They punished no one and went on sharing their message in a positive way.
They punished no one and went on sharing their message in a positive way
Yes. The editorial calls the killings gravely un-Islamic.
They asked the rulers to silence their critics
Not quite. The article says: They punished no one and went on sharing their message in a positive way.
They left the city where they were mocked
Not quite. The article says: They punished no one and went on sharing their message in a positive way.
questions.rationale: “Even during the Prophet’s time there were several instances of ridicule, however the Prophet and his Companions neither punished such persons nor asked anyone to do so.”

questions.article: Between Lesser Evil and Greater Evil
questions.q: The article distinguishes personal life from life in society. How do the choices differ?
options: In society one may demand the ideal; privately one must compromise
Not quite. The article says: Personally one may aim at the greatest good; in society the wise choice is often the lesser of two evils.
There is no difference between them
Not quite. The article says: Personally one may aim at the greatest good; in society the wise choice is often the lesser of two evils.
Personally one may aim at the greatest good; in society the wise choice is often the lesser of two evils
Right. “The wisdom to know the difference.”
In both, one should refuse anything imperfect
Not quite. The article says: Personally one may aim at the greatest good; in society the wise choice is often the lesser of two evils.
questions.rationale: “In one’s personal life, one can try to opt for the greater good. But, in society one has to be ready to opt for what seems to be the lesser evil.”

questions.article: Between Lesser Evil and Greater Evil
questions.q: What does the article identify as the “greater evil” to be avoided?
options: Unfavourable outward circumstances
Not quite. The article says: Negative thinking, which paralyses the mind and halts progress.
Lack of political power
Not quite. The article says: Negative thinking, which paralyses the mind and halts progress.
Being fewer in number
Not quite. The article says: Negative thinking, which paralyses the mind and halts progress.
Negative thinking, which paralyses the mind and halts progress
Yes. Unfavourable conditions are the lesser evil.
questions.rationale: “Unfavourable situations in terms of the result, are lesser evils. While, negative thinking, in terms of the result, is the greater evil.”

questions.q: The Caliph Umar said, “May God bless the man who sends me the gift of my own shortcoming.” What attitude does the article commend through this saying?
options: Eagerness to have one’s mistakes pointed out and to accept the truth
Exactly. The article calls accepting the truth the greatest act of worship.
Patience with people who talk too much
Not quite. The article says: Eagerness to have one’s mistakes pointed out and to accept the truth.
Generosity in giving presents
Not quite. The article says: Eagerness to have one’s mistakes pointed out and to accept the truth.
Suspicion of all praise
Not quite. The article says: Eagerness to have one’s mistakes pointed out and to accept the truth.
questions.rationale: “The highest point of this attribute is that man… eagerly awaits for someone to point out to him any shortcoming of his so that he may immediately accept it.”

questions.q: Why does the article say accepting the truth is so great an act?
options: It demands the sacrifice of one’s prestige and sense of greatness
Well read. And it is possible only where people may speak freely.
It is rewarded with public honour
Not quite. The article says: It demands the sacrifice of one’s prestige and sense of greatness.
It brings an end to all disagreement
Not quite. The article says: It demands the sacrifice of one’s prestige and sense of greatness.
It takes a great deal of study
Not quite. The article says: It demands the sacrifice of one’s prestige and sense of greatness.
questions.rationale: “This is the sacrifice of one’s prestige; of losing one’s greatness. To lose one’s sense of greatness for the sake of truth is an occasion when man earns his entry into heaven.”

questions.q: In the Prophet’s time, how were those who spoke against Islam answered?
options: With silence, by order
Not quite. The article says: With words – the poet Hassan was asked to reply in verse.
With banishment from the city
Not quite. The article says: With words – the poet Hassan was asked to reply in verse.
With words – the poet Hassan was asked to reply in verse
Yes. “Countering words with words.”
With a fine
Not quite. The article says: With words – the poet Hassan was asked to reply in verse.
questions.rationale: “The Prophet appointed a poet called Hassan to give a befitting answer in verse to the offenders, poetry being the main mode of public expression.”

questions.q: What does the article conclude about a person who lacks what is truly worth having – fear of God, remembrance, sincere piety?
options: It comes only in old age
Not quite. The article says: He has not really sought it, for God gives to those who ask.
God has decided to withhold it from him
Not quite. The article says: He has not really sought it, for God gives to those who ask.
He has not really sought it, for God gives to those who ask
Right. “Those who seek will always find.”
It is given only to a chosen few
Not quite. The article says: He has not really sought it, for God gives to those who ask.
questions.rationale: “If one does not have what is desirable in life, it means that one has not sought it… He gives only to those who ask.”

questions.article: The Straight Path for Social Living
questions.q: The Quran speaks of the Arabs being rescued “from the brink of an abyss of Fire.” What does the article take this to mean?
options: A volcano near Madinah
Not quite. The article says: The endless chain of revenge wars between the tribes.
The endless chain of revenge wars between the tribes
Yes. Each defeat bred a new war.
Poverty and famine
Not quite. The article says: The endless chain of revenge wars between the tribes.
The heat of the desert
Not quite. The article says: The endless chain of revenge wars between the tribes.
questions.rationale: “Because of this culture of seeking revenge, the Arab tribes were constantly engaged in a chain of wars. This chain of wars is referred to in the Quran as an ‘abyss of fire.’”

questions.q: What habit of mind does the article describe with the image of “waiting for a highway”?
options: Planning too carefully
Not quite. The article says: Putting off effort until ideal conditions arrive, and missing the opportunity already at hand.
Travelling too much
Not quite. The article says: Putting off effort until ideal conditions arrive, and missing the opportunity already at hand.
Putting off effort until ideal conditions arrive, and missing the opportunity already at hand
Correct. “Everyone is waiting for the train, which will never arrive.”
Relying on public transport
Not quite. The article says: Putting off effort until ideal conditions arrive, and missing the opportunity already at hand.
questions.rationale: “Don’t wait for the moment; instead every moment try to discover the opportunity that is already present, and avail it with wise planning.”

questions.q: The Kabah in Makkah had become a gathering place for all the tribes. How did the Prophet respond, according to the article?
options: He left the problem aside and used the gathering as a chance to convey his message
Well reasoned. This was the “third option.”
He moved the gathering to another town
Not quite. The article says: He left the problem aside and used the gathering as a chance to convey his message.
He called on his followers to clear it by force
Not quite. The article says: He left the problem aside and used the gathering as a chance to convey his message.
He stayed away from the Kabah altogether
Not quite. The article says: He left the problem aside and used the gathering as a chance to convey his message.
questions.rationale: “The Prophet ignored the problem and he tried to use the assembly for his mission of communicating the message of God to mankind.”
